rationale.answer_analysis: HR dropped and BP normalized.
rationale.common_trap: Assuming total recovery.
rationale.teaching_point: Monitor continuously.
rationale.safety_rationale: Fluid responsiveness proves intact cardiac function.

cases.title: Mateo Rivera: Diabetic Ketoacidosis With Hypokalemia N - Group A
cases.topic: Diabetic ketoacidosis in an adolescent with type 1 diabetes
cases.clinical_focus: Prioritize dehydration, acidosis, and potassium safety during DKA treatment rather than focusing only on hyperglycemia.
cases.client_needs: Physiological Adaptation; Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies; Reduction of Risk Potential

patient.name: Mateo Rivera
patient.past_medical_history: Type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 9; insulin pump therapy
patient.social_history: Plays soccer; mother reports pump alarmed overnight and client had vomiting

timeline.text: Initial pediatric ED assessment shows dehydration, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul respirations.
Client becomes more lethargic with persistent tachypnea and hypotension.
Labs confirm DKA with severe acidosis and low potassium.
DKA orders focus on fluids and potassium before insulin.
Potassium replacement is underway and insulin is held temporarily for safety.
After insulin initiation, glucose and symptoms improve but acidosis persists.

overview.situation: Adolescent with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria, and weakness after insulin pump malfunction.
overview.chief_complaint: My stomach hurts and I keep throwing up.
overview.chief_concern_card: Vomiting, Kussmaul respirations, dehydration, and possible DKA.

ehr.history_physical: Case Summary: Mateo Rivera is a 14-year-old male with type 1 diabetes who presents after insulin pump malfunction with vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria, dehydration, and deep rapid respirations concerning for DKA. Chief Concern Card: Hyperglycemia with dehydration and acidosis risk. Focused exam shows dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, fruity breath, diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding, and Kussmaul respirations.

notes.note: Client reports vomiting four times overnight and states his insulin pump alarmed for occlusion. He appears drowsy but follows commands and asks for water repeatedly.
Client becomes more lethargic and respirations remain deep and rapid. Mucous membranes are very dry and capillary refill is 4 seconds.
Point-of-care glucose reads high and serum labs are sent before insulin is prepared. Provider is notified that potassium is low with severe acidosis.
Normal saline bolus is complete and potassium replacement is infusing on a cardiac monitor. Insulin infusion is held until potassium is safely above the protocol threshold.
Client is easier to arouse and reports less abdominal pain after fluids and insulin initiation. Glucose is falling but the anion gap remains elevated.

orders.order: 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg IV bolus, then maintenance fluids per DKA protocol.
Add potassium to IV fluids and place on cardiac monitor.
Hold regular insulin infusion until potassium is greater than 3.3 mEq/L.
Point-of-care glucose every hour and basic metabolic panel every 2 hours.
Start regular insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hr once potassium is 3.6 mEq/L.

diagnostics.result: Large ketones and glucose present.
Sinus tachycardia without peaked T waves.

ehr.history_physical: Case Summary: Denise Walker is a 58-year-old female with diabetes, hypertension, and smoking history who presents with chest pressure, jaw radiation, nausea, diaphoresis, and evolving ECG changes concerning for inferior STEMI. Chief Concern Card: Ischemic chest pressure with diaphoresis and high cardiovascular risk. Focused exam shows cool clammy skin, no wheezing, equal pulses, and no focal neurologic deficit.

notes.note: Client reports 8 out of 10 substernal pressure radiating to the jaw with nausea. She is pale and diaphoretic but speaking clearly.
A 12-lead ECG is completed within 10 minutes of arrival and shows ST elevation in inferior leads. Client becomes more anxious and states the pressure is not improving.
Provider reviews ECG and activates the cath lab team. The nurse confirms no aspirin allergy or recent erectile dysfunction medication use before administering ordered medications.
Client reports pain decreased to 4 out of 10 after aspirin and nitroglycerin while cath lab transfer is being arranged. Blood pressure is lower but remains above the ordered safety parameter.
Client returns from percutaneous coronary intervention with right radial access dressing intact. Chest pressure is 1 out of 10 and ECG changes have partially resolved.

orders.order: Chew aspirin 324 mg now if no allergy.
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual every 5 minutes up to 3 doses if systolic blood pressure remains above 100 mm Hg.
Heparin bolus and infusion per ACS protocol.
Activate cath lab and prepare for immediate PCI.
Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 90% or respiratory distress develops.

diagnostics.result: ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL.
Right coronary artery occlusion treated with drug-eluting stent.

rationale.summary: Immediate solutions are **epinephrine, stopping exposure, oxygen, IV fluids, and airway readiness**; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.
rationale.answer_analysis:

- **row_b (Immediate life-saving)**: Stopping exposure prevents ongoing reaction and IV access supports resuscitation.
- **row_c (Immediate life-saving)**: Airway and oxygenation support are critical.

options.text: Stop the ceftriaxone infusion and call for emergency help
options.rationale: The trigger must be stopped and additional help is required.

options.text: Administer IM epinephrine into the mid-outer thigh
options.rationale: Epinephrine is the priority medication.

options.rationale: This supports airway and circulation.

options.rationale: Fluids address hypotension.

options.rationale: Adjuncts follow epinephrine and resuscitation priorities.

options.rationale: Stop the infusion but maintain IV access for fluids and emergency medications.

rationale.summary: The safest sequence removes the trigger, mobilizes help, gives **IM epinephrine immediately**, supports oxygenation/circulation, then gives adjuncts.
rationale.answer_analysis:
- **step_1 (Correct)**: The trigger must be stopped and additional help is required.
- **step_2 (Correct)**: Epinephrine is the priority medication.
- **step_3 (Correct)**: This supports airway and circulation.
- **step_4 (Correct)**: Fluids address hypotension.
- **step_5 (Correct)**: Adjuncts follow epinephrine and resuscitation priorities.
- **distractor_a (Incorrect)**: Diphenhydramine does not reverse airway edema or shock and must not precede epinephrine.
- **distractor_b (Incorrect)**: Documentation is required later but must not delay life-saving treatment.
- **distractor_c (Incorrect)**: Stop the infusion but maintain IV access for fluids and emergency medications.

rationale.teaching_point: In anaphylaxis, epinephrine should be near the front of the sequence every time.
rationale.safety_rationale: Delaying epinephrine for IV placement or adjunct medications is unsafe.

ehr.history_physical: Case Summary: Gerald Kim is a 67-year-old male with atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation who presents 65 minutes after sudden aphasia, right facial droop, and right arm weakness concerning for acute ischemic stroke. Chief Concern Card: Sudden focal neurologic deficit with known last well time. Focused exam shows expressive aphasia, right facial droop, right arm drift to bed, right leg weakness, and intact airway.

notes.note: Client arrives with expressive aphasia, right facial droop, and right arm weakness. Spouse states symptoms began suddenly at 0710 and he was normal before breakfast.
Stroke alert is activated and point-of-care glucose is normal. Client remains awake but cannot name objects and follows simple commands inconsistently.
Noncontrast head CT is completed and shows no intracranial hemorrhage. Blood pressure remains above the thrombolytic treatment parameter and the provider gives antihypertensive orders.
Labetalol is administered and blood pressure improves below the ordered threshold. Thrombolytic consent discussion is completed by the provider and the medication is prepared per protocol.
Client has improved right arm movement and can say short phrases after thrombolytic infusion. He denies headache and no new bleeding is observed.

orders.order: Keep NPO until swallow screen is completed.
Administer labetalol 10 mg IV now to lower BP before thrombolytic therapy.
Prepare thrombolytic medication per stroke protocol if BP is below treatment threshold and no contraindications are present.
Neurologic assessments and vital signs per post-thrombolytic protocol.
Do not administer aspirin or anticoagulants for 24 hours after thrombolytic therapy unless specifically ordered.

diagnostics.result: Score 14 with aphasia, facial droop, right arm drift, and right leg weakness.
No acute intracranial hemorrhage.
Atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response.

ehr.history_physical: Case Summary: Maya Thompson is a 45-year-old female taking lithium who develops coarse tremor, diarrhea, nausea, ataxia, dehydration, elevated lithium level, and acute kidney stress after gastroenteritis and ibuprofen use. Chief Concern Card: Tremor and unsteady gait in a client taking lithium with dehydration. Focused exam shows dry mucous membranes, coarse bilateral hand tremor, mild confusion about the date, unsteady tandem gait, and no suicidal ideation.

notes.note: Client reports three days of diarrhea, poor fluid intake, nausea, and worsening hand tremor. She took ibuprofen twice daily for migraine and continued lithium because she did not want her mood to worsen.
Client is unsteady when walking to the bathroom and needs staff assistance to prevent a fall. Tremor is coarse and she has difficulty holding a cup without spilling.
Provider is notified of elevated lithium level and kidney function changes. Lithium is held and fall precautions are implemented while IV fluids are started.
Client reports nausea is improving and gait is steadier with assistance. Tremor is still present but less severe after hydration.
Client correctly explains several lithium safety rules but makes one unsafe statement about salt restriction. Repeat lithium level is therapeutic and creatinine is improving.

orders.order: Hold lithium and notify psychiatry and primary provider.
Start 0.9% sodium chloride IV fluids and encourage oral fluids as tolerated.
Institute fall precautions and assist with ambulation.
Avoid NSAIDs and thiazide diuretics; review medication list for interactions.
Repeat lithium level, creatinine, sodium, and neurologic assessment.

ehr.history_physical: Case Summary: Maya Thompson is a 45-year-old female taking lithium who develops coarse tremor, diarrhea, nausea, ataxia, dehydration, elevated lithium level, and acute kidney stress after gastroenteritis and ibuprofen use. Chief Concern Card: Tremor and unsteady gait in a client taking lithium with dehydration. Focused exam shows dry mucous membranes, coarse bilateral hand tremor, mild confusion about the date, unsteady tandem gait, and no suicidal ideation.

notes.note: Client reports three days of diarrhea, poor fluid intake, nausea, and worsening hand tremor. She took ibuprofen twice daily for migraine and continued lithium because she did not want her mood to worsen.
Client is unsteady when walking to the bathroom and needs staff assistance to prevent a fall. Tremor is coarse and she has difficulty holding a cup without spilling.

options.text: I will call my provider if I have vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or cannot keep fluids down.
options.rationale: This statement is correct and shows good sick-day understanding.

options.text: I should keep my salt and fluid intake consistent unless my provider changes the plan.
options.rationale: This is correct lithium safety teaching.

options.text: If my hands start shaking badly, I will take ibuprofen and skip drinking water.
options.rationale: This is unsafe because NSAIDs and dehydration can worsen lithium toxicity.

options.rationale: This is correct monitoring behavior.

options.rationale: This is unsafe because sodium depletion can increase lithium retention.

options.text: I will not restart lithium until the provider tells me to.
options.rationale: This is correct after toxicity.

rationale.summary: The unsafe statements involve **NSAID use, dehydration, and severe sodium restriction**, all of which increase lithium toxicity risk.
rationale.answer_analysis:
- **stmt_a (Incorrect)**: This statement is correct and shows good sick-day understanding.
- **stmt_b (Incorrect)**: This is correct lithium safety teaching.
- **stmt_c (Correct)**: This is unsafe because NSAIDs and dehydration can worsen lithium toxicity.
- **stmt_d (Incorrect)**: This is correct monitoring behavior.
- **stmt_e (Correct)**: This is unsafe because sodium depletion can increase lithium retention.
- **stmt_f (Incorrect)**: This is correct after toxicity.
rationale.common_trap: Blood pressure advice and pain relief advice can conflict with lithium safety. Teaching must be medication-specific, not generic.
rationale.teaching_point: For lithium, consistent sodium and hydration are protective.
rationale.safety_rationale: Discharging without correcting these statements invites recurrent toxicity and falls.

end_of_case_debrief.clinical_judgment_map: Diarrhea, poor intake, tremor, ataxia, lithium use, NSAID and thiazide exposure, lithium level 1.9, creatinine 1.6, and sodium 130 led to holding lithium, isotonic fluids, fall precautions, interaction teaching, and repeat monitoring.
end_of_case_debrief.missed_cues: A weaker learner may miss ibuprofen and thiazide interactions or teach sodium restriction incorrectly.
end_of_case_debrief.priority_trap: Thinking adherence means continuing lithium through dehydration.
end_of_case_debrief.safety_lesson: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range and is highly sensitive to hydration, sodium balance, renal function, and interacting drugs.
end_of_case_debrief.outcome_interpretation: Lithium level, creatinine, sodium, gait, and nausea improved, but unsafe teaching statements required correction.
end_of_case_debrief.next_time_rule: Lithium safety is hydration, consistent salt, lab monitoring, and calling during illness.

patient.name: Marisol Vega
patient.admission_diagnosis: Upper GI Bleed With Hypovolemic Shock
patient.social_history: Lives with spouse and uses ibuprofen several times daily for knee pain. Drinks one glass of wine with dinner most evenings.

timeline.text: Client arrives pale and diaphoretic after coffee-ground emesis. She reports black stools for two days and dizziness when standing.
Client becomes more restless and asks repeatedly where she is. Large black stool is noted in the bedside commode.
Type and crossmatch specimen is sent and two large-bore IV catheters are inserted. Provider is notified of hypotension, tachycardia, and suspected active bleeding.
Packed red blood cells arrive from blood bank and pantoprazole infusion is started. Gastroenterology is notified for urgent endoscopy after stabilization.
Client reports less dizziness after transfusion begins. Blood pressure improves but urine output remains low.
Client is more alert and denies further emesis. Repeat hemoglobin is lower than baseline and endoscopy is still pending.

patient.name: Noah Bennett
patient.past_medical_history: Type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at age 9
patient.social_history: Lives with parents and plays soccer. Family reports recent influenza symptoms and missed insulin doses.

timeline.text: Adolescent arrives with parent after two days of vomiting and missed insulin. He is lethargic but opens eyes to voice and answers slowly.
Client has deep rapid respirations and reports worsening abdominal pain. Capillary refill is delayed and mucous membranes are very dry.
Serum chemistry and venous blood gas are resulted. Provider orders fluid resuscitation, potassium monitoring, and insulin infusion after potassium safety is confirmed.

patient.past_medical_history: Severe COPD, home oxygen at night, hypertension
patient.social_history: Former smoker with 45 pack-year history. Daughter reports increased sputum and sleepiness for two days.

timeline.text: Client arrives with worsening dyspnea and green sputum. She is drowsy but follows commands when spoken to loudly.
Oxygen is applied and wheezing persists after the first nebulizer treatment. Daughter reports the client has been harder to wake today.
Arterial blood gas and chest x-ray results are reviewed by the provider. Orders are entered for controlled oxygen, bronchodilators, antibiotics, steroids, and possible noninvasive ventilation.
Client is placed on bilevel positive airway pressure after worsening carbon dioxide retention. She tolerates the mask with coaching.
Client is more alert and accessory muscle use decreases. Wheezing persists but air movement is improved.
Client remains awake and answers questions appropriately. Oxygen saturation is within target but carbon dioxide remains elevated.
